question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man sits upright in the pre-operative bay awaiting transfer to the minimally invasive suite for a planned laparoscopic right hemicolectomy with intracorporeal anastomosis, a procedure the colorectal attending estimates will require two hours of pneumoperitoneum under general endotracheal anesthesia and an anticipated three-night postoperative stay. The surgical indication is an endoscopically tattooed, obstructing adenocarcinoma of the hepatic flexure discovered on colonoscopy six weeks ago after he presented with iron-deficiency anemia and intermittent crampy pain; staging CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no distant disease, and he has not yet undergone any abdominal operation for this malignancy. His oncologic work-up at that time included insertion of a power-injectable, single-lumen portacath in the right pectoral region to facilitate perioperative chemotherapy; the device remains in situ beneath an intact transparent dressing, flushes with minimal resistance, and returns dark venous blood. Beyond diagnostic colonoscopy and the port placement, he has not been to an operating room, endoscopy suite, or interventional radiology table in the past month, and has therefore undergone no major surgical procedures during that period. The medical record does recount a neurologic event two and a half weeks ago when he developed an abrupt left visual field deficit while shopping; paramedics transported him to a primary stroke center where diffusion-weighted MRI demonstrated a small right posterior cerebral artery infarct. Symptoms improved to near-baseline after intravenous thrombolysis, and he completed inpatient rehabilitation with only subtle residual inattention on detailed neuropsychologic testing. Neurology cleared him for non-emergent surgery provided blood pressure is well controlled and antiplatelet therapy is held on the morning of the operation; thus his aspirin 81 mg was stopped three days ago. He otherwise reports no episodes of heart-failure decompensation, exertional chest tightness, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, longstanding wheeze, chronic cough, intestinal inflammatory flares, or systemic infection requiring intravenous antibiotics during the last month. During this same timeframe he has not developed pneumonia, sepsis, or an acute myocardial infarction, and he has never been given a formal diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. There have been no casts, splints, or fractures involving the pelvis or long bones, and he denies any high-energy trauma, spinal injury, or prolonged immobilization—until arriving at the hospital yesterday evening for bowel preparation he maintained his usual routine of brisk one-mile walks with the family dog each morning. He has never experienced swelling, tenderness, or erythema of either calf, has not required anticoagulation in the past, and knows of no relatives with “clotting problems.” Medications at the bedside include lisinopril 10 mg daily for well-controlled hypertension, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and a three-month tapering schedule of clopidogrel that was discontinued after the stroke but had been used only briefly; no glucocorticoids, hormonal agents, erythropoiesis stimulators, or corticosteroid inhalers are listed. He quit a 20-pack-year cigarette habit 15 years ago, drinks two beers on weekends, and denies recreational drug use; body mass index calculated this morning is 25 kg m⁻². On inspection he appears comfortable, answers questions fully, and is oriented to time, place, and situation. Vital signs thirty minutes ago: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/72 mm Hg, pulse 70 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Airway evaluation reveals Mallampati class II view, full cervical extension, intact dentition, and a thyromental distance of three fingerbreadths. Carotid upstrokes are brisk, jugular venous contour is not elevated, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, extra sounds, or rubs. Lung fields are clear to auscultation throughout with good air entry and no wheezes or crackles. Abdominal exam shows a soft, non-distended belly with mild right-sided colonic tympany from bowel prep; no organomegaly or peritoneal signs are elicited. Extremities are warm with brisk capillary refill; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally, calf circumferences measure 36 cm on each side, and the skin surface is smooth without bulging tortuous veins (varicosities), pitting edema, or tenderness to compressive palpation. Strength testing demonstrates 5/5 power in all four limbs, sensation is intact, and a brief confrontation test detects only a subtle left homonymous quadrantanopia consistent with the prior infarct. Indwelling vascular access includes the previously described chest port connected to a heplock extension as well as a new 18-gauge peripheral intravenous catheter in the left antecubital fossa running Lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; no additional catheters, drains, or urinary devices are present. Pre-induction laboratory studies drawn at 05:30 through the port reveal hemoglobin 13.9 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 41 %, platelet count 248 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 6.7 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.2 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.91 mg dL⁻¹, AST 22 U L⁻¹, ALT 24 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.6 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.1 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram printed on arrival shows normal sinus rhythm at 68 beats min⁻¹, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 96 ms, and no acute ST-T wave changes. Posterior-anterior chest radiograph taken yesterday demonstrates clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette, and appropriate port catheter tip position over the cavo-atrial junction. Sequential pneumatic compression sleeves are wrapped around both calves but remain inactive pending induction, pharmacologic venous prophylaxis has been deferred until skin closure, and he has been nil per os since midnight, having completed his polyethylene glycol solution at 22:00.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score sums weighted patient and procedural risk factors at the preoperative assessment.
- Age 59 (41–60 years): 1 point.
- Planned laparoscopic hemicolectomy lasting 2 hours (>45 minutes): 2 points. Count the operation once.
- Active colon adenocarcinoma: 2 points.
- Central venous access via an indwelling chest port: 2 points. The peripheral IV adds nothing.
- Ischemic stroke 2.5 weeks ago (within 1 month): 5 points, even though symptoms improved.
- BMI is exactly 25, not >25. He was ambulatory, with no other qualifying recent major surgery, prior VTE, known thrombophilia, or additional documented risk factor: 0 points.
Total = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 5 = 12.
Final answer: 12
